title: I Tried to Fool a Scientific Publisher With AI
gist: A journalist 'vibe-researched' an optical-solitons paper with free ChatGPT/Gemini and then had Analemma's autonomous FARS system do real computational research and write a paper; IEEE Access caught both (ghost citations; excessive preprint references and figure artifacts). The piece documents the scale of AI slop (57% of 2025 papers show LLM influence), peer-review strain, and a debate over provenance-based trust versus AI-driven review as autonomous research systems scale. The headline says 'I Tried to Fool a Scientific Publisher With AI' while the text's own headline reads 'I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper'.

themes.theme: Scale of AI slop in publishing

insights.claim: An estimated 57% of academic articles published by 2025 showed detectable evidence of LLM influence, up from 12% in 2023.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: LLM penetration of the scientific record is near-majority, undermining the reliability of literature as an input for R&D and AI training data.
insights.quote: By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence

insights.claim: Over 12% of Nature Communications peer reviews in 2025 were found to be completely AI-generated.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: AI is penetrating the quality-control layer itself, not just submissions.

insights.claim: For every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI use in 2025, only one formally disclosed it, so measured LLM involvement likely grossly understates reality.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Disclosure regimes are failing ~40:1, so detection/verification tooling rather than self-reporting will be the binding control.

insights.claim: Some estimates suggest hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Fraud volume is large enough to create a sizeable market for research-integrity screening.

insights.claim: IEEE's research-integrity manager argues AI slop is eroding trust not just in the scientific record but in science as a whole.
insights.speaker: Amanda Sulicz
insights.so_what: Trust erosion raises the value of provenance and verification layers in scholarly publishing.
insights.quote: AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.

insights.claim: A non-expert using only free ChatGPT (GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini 3 Flash, without editing output, produced a realistic-looking optical-solitons paper in IEEE Access style with roughly two dozen prompts.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: The cost of producing a superficially plausible fake paper has collapsed to near zero, so submission volume pressure will keep rising.

insights.claim: When one chatbot refused to fabricate research, switching to the other model or asking what the next step would look like 'hypothetically' usually bypassed the refusal; ChatGPT was more resistant than Gemini.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Model-level guardrails are easily circumvented by model-hopping, so safeguards must sit at the publisher/verification layer.

insights.claim: The free-LLM fake contained no 'tortured phrases', and remaining AI stylistic tics (hedging, groups of three, formulaic transitions) are hard to flag because unimaginative humans use them too.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Stylometric AI-detection is a weak moat; detection vendors relying on text style face eroding efficacy.

insights.claim: IEEE Access's automated integrity checks caught the fake quickly because of hallucinated 'ghost citations': STM Integrity Hub flagged 12, and a MolecularConnections checker could not validate 24 references.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Reference validation is today's most effective automated defense and a concrete product category for integrity tooling.

insights.claim: The managing editor of IEEE Access found nothing majorly scientifically wrong in the fake, but said the number of hallucinated references cast doubt on the whole work.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Content-level review by non-specialists cannot catch plausible fakes; metadata checks do the work.
insights.quote: It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.

insights.claim: A domain expert found the fake professionally written but flagged dense math needing specialist evaluation, excessive acronyms, and a few confidently stated physics claims that were at best debatable.
insights.speaker: Gaetano Assanto
insights.so_what: Catching AI fakes on substance requires scarce specialist reviewer time.

insights.claim: More advanced LLMs no longer make the kinds of mistakes (like ghost citations) that free models make, implying today's reference-based catch will not hold.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Current integrity defenses have a short shelf life; expect an ongoing detection arms race.

insights.claim: IEEE's director of publishing ethics warns that a detection tool built today may not work against the AI-created paper of tomorrow.
insights.speaker: Luigi Longobardi
insights.so_what: Detection-only strategies are structurally losing; durable value shifts to provenance and source verification.
insights.quote: It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow

insights.claim: Peer review processed well over 3 million papers in 2022, before AI tools became ubiquitous, and was already near breaking point.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: The volunteer review system lacks capacity to absorb AI-driven submission growth.
insights.locator: Even before AI tools became ubiquitous

insights.claim: IEEE Access receives about 60,000 submissions a year and accepts about 20% (~12,000), each reviewed by at least two independent reviewers.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Shows the scale of triage burden at a single large open-access journal.

insights.claim: The average number of reviewer invitations IEEE Access must send per article has risen 50% since 2018.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Reviewer scarcity is a quantifiable, worsening bottleneck that raises publishing costs and timelines.

insights.claim: The root cause is publish-or-perish culture, which drives incremental output and the use of paper mills; AI amplifies these existing dynamics rather than creating them.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Fixing the problem requires incentive change, not just tooling, so the slop problem will persist.
insights.locator: Even before AI tools became ubiquitous

insights.claim: Retraction Watch's cofounder frames publish-or-perish as kindling, paper mills as gasoline and AI as the accelerant, and sees the volume crisis as a possible catalyst for first-principles reform.
insights.speaker: Ivan Oransky
insights.so_what: Crisis may force structural reform of publishing business models and incentives.
insights.quote: publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant

insights.claim: Even integrity watchdogs are hit: Ivan Oransky has found fabricated references attributed to him, including in an article criticizing post-publication peer review.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Ghost citations pollute citation graphs and author reputations, distorting bibliometrics.
insights.locator: Even the people who track problems

insights.claim: Autonomous research systems such as FARS, AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher and DeepScientist can, from a single prompt, do literature review, propose research, run digital experiments and write a full paper with no further human input.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: A competitive category of 'AI scientist' platforms is forming, targeting human attention as the bottleneck in R&D.

insights.claim: LabClaw links autonomous research to autonomous labs that generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery, pushing AI research beyond purely digital experiments.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Coupling AI agents to self-driving labs extends automation into wet-lab R&D, relevant to biotech productivity.
insights.locator: Very recent systems are even beginning

insights.claim: FARS, from Singapore startup Analemma, produced 166 papers in 417 hours; Analemma was acquired by Baidu during reporting and the online FARS service was discontinued.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Big Tech is acquiring autonomous-research startups, signalling strategic interest in AI-driven science.

insights.claim: FARS is an agentic orchestration system, not an LLM, using four specialized agents (ideation, planning, experiment, writing) on a compute cluster that can call any open- or closed-source LLM.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Value accrues to orchestration layers that are model-agnostic, commoditizing underlying LLMs.
insights.locator: Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine

insights.claim: In the test, FARS produced a research proposal with an extremely detailed literature review in 21 minutes, completed the experiment by the next day, and wrote a submission-ready paper in 2 hours.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Research cycle times compress from months to roughly a day, implying an explosion of paper volume.

insights.claim: The FARS paper's only giveaway was an auto-inserted warning line below the abstract, which the author simply deleted before submission.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Voluntary AI-disclosure watermarks in text are trivially removable and offer no real protection.
insights.quote: WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.
insights.locator: At this point, I finally had

insights.claim: The FARS paper had no fake references but would have been rejected for a very high share of preprint citations, which the editor attributes to the dataset the AI accesses; she also spotted a nonsense figure label 'lhewl' and AI artifacts that integrity tools missed.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: AI-research outputs inherit biases of their training/retrieval corpora, and figure checks still rely on humans.

insights.claim: Papers from an AI Scientist system and the Autoscience Institute passed double-blind peer review at the International Conference on Learning Representations in 2025.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: AI-generated research is already clearing top-venue peer review, validating the category.

insights.claim: As autonomous research systems improve and produce outputs at volume, the author expects the waves to build into a tsunami threatening today's scientific and publishing process.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: Incumbent journal publishing models face disruption from machine-scale output.

themes.theme: Future of the paper and trust

insights.claim: Analemma argues FARS challenges the paper as the unit of knowledge and that the future looks like a living knowledge graph of well-scoped human and machine contributions.
insights.speaker: Xiwen Su
insights.so_what: If the paper unit dissolves, journal-centric publishers' business models are at risk while knowledge-graph platforms gain.
insights.quote: FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge

insights.claim: Su predicts line-by-line peer review will disappear, with automated systems handling reproducibility, statistics and novelty screening while humans judge whether research matters.
insights.speaker: Xiwen Su
insights.so_what: Opens a market for automated review/validation services.
insights.locator: In this future, humans will continue

insights.claim: IEEE Access already automates triage such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submissions and reference validity, and uses AI semantic search to match manuscripts to reviewers.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Publishers are active buyers of AI triage tooling.

insights.claim: Mahoney argues AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, but contends humans must stay at the wheel and the key question is whether work can be trusted and reproduced.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Reproducibility and trust become the core value proposition, favoring verification infrastructure.
insights.quote: The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?

insights.claim: Longobardi suggests scientists may need to prove how they discovered results, for example by integrating lab equipment with blockchain-based trust markers recording who generated what data and when.
insights.speaker: Luigi Longobardi
insights.so_what: Points to demand for research-provenance infrastructure (lab instrumentation, ELNs, possibly blockchain attestation).

insights.claim: Early provenance efforts exist: two Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces departments assign every sample a unique ID and QR code, and Southampton's School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering rolled out an electronic lab notebook system.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
entities: Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces
insights.so_what: Lab-data provenance tools (sample tracking, ELNs) gain a new integrity-driven adoption driver.

insights.claim: The author concludes that deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become harder than detecting outright fraud.
insights.speaker: IEEE Spectrum
insights.so_what: The core problem shifts from fraud detection to legitimacy/provenance standards for AI-produced research.
